  name   = "cover-processor-${data.archive_file.cover_processor.output_md5}.zip"
  bucket = google_storage_bucket.function_source.name
  source = data.archive_file.cover_processor.output_path
}

resource "google_service_account" "cover_processor" {
  project      = var.project_id
  account_id   = "cover-processor-${var.environment}"
  display_name = "Bookshelf cover-processor"
}

# The Cloud Storage service agent must be able to publish to Pub/Sub for the trigger to work.
data "google_storage_project_service_account" "gcs" {
  project = var.project_id
}

resource "google_project_iam_member" "gcs_publisher" {
  project = var.project_id
  role    = "roles/pubsub.publisher"
  member  = "serviceAccount:${data.google_storage_project_service_account.gcs.email_address}"
}

# Roles the function's service account needs to be invoked by Eventarc and to pull its image.
resource "google_project_iam_member" "cover_processor" {
  for_each = toset([
    "roles/run.invoker",
    "roles/eventarc.eventReceiver",
    "roles/artifactregistry.reader",
  ])

  project = var.project_id
  role    = each.key
  member  = google_service_account.cover_processor.member
}

resource "google_pubsub_topic" "cover_events" {
  project                    = var.project_id
  name                       = "bookshelf-${var.environment}-cover-events"
  message_retention_duration = "86400s"
}

resource "google_pubsub_topic_iam_member" "cover_processor_publisher" {
  project = var.project_id
  topic   = google_pubsub_topic.cover_events.name
  role    = "roles/pubsub.publisher"
  member  = google_service_account.cover_processor.member
}

resource "google_cloudfunctions2_function" "cover_processor" {
  project  = var.project_id
  name     = "cover-processor"
  location = var.region

  build_config {
    runtime     = "python313"
    entry_point = "process_cover"

    source {
      storage_source {
        bucket = google_storage_bucket.function_source.name
        object = google_storage_bucket_object.cover_processor.name
      }
    }
  }

  service_config {
    min_instance_count             = 0
    max_instance_count             = 5
    available_memory               = "512Mi"
    timeout_seconds                = 120
    ingress_settings               = "ALLOW_INTERNAL_ONLY"
    all_traffic_on_latest_revision = true
    service_account_email          = google_service_account.cover_processor.email

    environment_variables = {
      EVENTS_TOPIC = google_pubsub_topic.cover_events.id
    }
  }

  event_trigger {
    trigger_region        = var.region
    event_type            = "google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized"
    retry_policy          = "RETRY_POLICY_RETRY"
    service_account_email = google_service_account.cover_processor.email

    event_filters {
      attribute = "bucket"
      value     = google_storage_bucket.covers.name
    }
  }

  depends_on = [
    google_project_iam_member.gcs_publisher,
    google_project_iam_member.cover_processor,
  ]
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_cloudfunctions2_function and Cloud Run functions — Runtime support

The event, the IAM roles and the ordering follow the provider’s own Cloud Storage example. Some more points:

  • The trigger location must match the bucket location: the provider’s example notes that the trigger must be in the same location as the bucket, which is why trigger_region and the covers bucket both use var.region.

  • The Cloud Storage service agent is created on demand; use the google_storage_project_service_account data source to obtain its address instead of constructing it.

  • The build runs as a service account of its own, which build_config.service_account can set; give it a dedicated account with only the permissions to build and write images, rather than relying on defaults.

  • Zip names that include the content hash (as above) make the function redeploy whenever the code changes, which a fixed object name would not.

  • The archive provider (hashicorp/archive) is needed for the data source; add it to required_providers.

The BigQuery half has more to say about identity than about code. A BigQuery subscription is a Pub/Sub subscription with a bigquery_config block: Pub/Sub writes each message into the table without a consumer, either to a single data column, or, with use_table_schema, into the columns of the table, in which case messages must be JSON. Which identity writes is selected with service_account_email; the documented default is the Pub/Sub service agent, but a dedicated account is easier to audit and to grant narrowly.

resource "google_bigquery_dataset" "analytics" {
  project                    = var.project_id
  dataset_id                 = "bookshelf_analytics"
  location                   = var.region
  delete_contents_on_destroy = false

  labels = {
    component = "analytics"
  }
}

resource "google_bigquery_table" "cover_events" {
  project             = var.project_id
  dataset_id          = google_bigquery_dataset.analytics.dataset_id
  table_id            = "cover_events"
  deletion_protection = true

  time_partitioning {
    type  = "DAY"
    field = "processed_at"
  }

  schema = jsonencode([
    { name = "book_id", type = "STRING", mode = "REQUIRED" },
    { name = "object_name", type = "STRING", mode = "REQUIRED" },
    { name = "width", type = "INT64", mode = "NULLABLE" },
    { name = "height", type = "INT64", mode = "NULLABLE" },
    { name = "processed_at", type = "TIMESTAMP", mode = "REQUIRED" },
  ])
}

resource "google_service_account" "pubsub_bigquery" {
  project      = var.project_id
  account_id   = "pubsub-bq-${var.environment}"
  display_name = "Pub/Sub to BigQuery writer"
}

resource "google_project_iam_member" "pubsub_bigquery" {
  for_each = toset(["roles/bigquery.metadataViewer", "roles/bigquery.dataEditor"])

  project = var.project_id
  role    = each.key
  member  = google_service_account.pubsub_bigquery.member
}

resource "google_pubsub_subscription" "cover_events_bigquery" {
  project = var.project_id
  name    = "cover-events-to-bigquery"
  topic   = google_pubsub_topic.cover_events.id

  bigquery_config {
    table                 = "${google_bigquery_table.cover_events.project}.${google_bigquery_table.cover_events.dataset_id}.${google_bigquery_table.cover_events.table_id}"
    use_table_schema      = true
    drop_unknown_fields   = true
    service_account_email = google_service_account.pubsub_bigquery.email
  }

  depends_on = [google_project_iam_member.pubsub_bigquery]
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_pubsub_subscription, google_bigquery_table and google_bigquery_dataset

deletion_protection on google_bigquery_table is enabled unless it is set, so destroying a table needs two steps: set it to false, apply, then destroy. drop_unknown_fields makes Pub/Sub discard message fields that are not columns of the table; without it, messages with extra fields stay in the backlog. A topic, subscription or table that changes shape should be treated as a migration, not as an in-place edit.

Service accounts and keys

Wang creates service accounts and downloads JSON keys. The right default today is: create service accounts with google_service_account, grant roles with the non-authoritative google_project_iam_member, and never create keys. A google_service_account_key resource stores the private key in state and produces a credential that does not expire; every use case that seems to need one has a keyless alternative:

Need Keyless alternative

Terraform on a laptop

ADC with impersonation of the deployer account.

Terraform in CI

Workload Identity Federation, see above.

Code running on Google Cloud

The service account attached to Cloud Run, the VM or the function.

Code running elsewhere

Workload Identity Federation with the platform’s identity provider.

A short-lived token for a script

The google_service_account_access_token or google_service_account_id_token ephemeral resource, or gcloud auth print-access-token --impersonate-service-account.

Source: Google Cloud — Best practices for security and Terraform Registry — google_service_account_key

Granting the Owner, Editor or Viewer basic roles to a service account is explicitly discouraged in production by Google’s authentication documentation; use predefined or custom roles scoped to what the account does. The IAM resources are covered in the next major section.

GKE

Wang provisions a GKE cluster with node pools, add-ons, network policy and the Kubernetes provider to create a Service, an Ingress and RBAC objects. The Kubernetes half moves to Docker, Kubernetes and Helm Providers, including the two-phase apply problem when a provider is configured from a cluster that does not exist yet, and the guidance to hand application delivery to Helm or GitOps (see the Kubernetes section). What belongs here is the cluster itself:

resource "google_container_cluster" "bookshelf" {
  project  = var.project_id
  name     = "bookshelf-${var.environment}"
  location = var.region

  enable_autopilot    = true
  deletion_protection = true

  network    = google_compute_network.bookshelf.id
  subnetwork = google_compute_subnetwork.bookshelf["app"].id

  release_channel {
    channel = "REGULAR"
  }

  private_cluster_config {
    enable_private_nodes = true
  }

  master_authorized_networks_config {
    cidr_blocks {
      cidr_block   = "203.0.113.0/24"
      display_name = "office-vpn"
    }
  }

  ip_allocation_policy {}
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_container_cluster

An Autopilot cluster has no node pools to manage and applies hardened defaults; use Standard clusters only when you need node-level control, and then create node pools as separate google_container_node_pool resources with remove_default_node_pool. The range 203.0.113.0/24 is a documentation address; the point is that authorized networks should list real administrator ranges, never 0.0.0.0/0, which defeats the control. deletion_protection is a google_container_cluster argument too. The provider’s own guide on GKE (using_gke_with_terraform) and the section GKE clusters cover node pools, upgrades and networking in depth.

Secrets, security and resilience

The second half of the rebuild is about what must not leak and what must survive. It follows the same layers: secrets and keys in the data layer, IAM in every layer, and logging, alerts and recovery in the observability layer. The general mechanics of sensitive values (the sensitive flag, ephemeral values, write-only arguments, state encryption) are in Sensitive Data, Ephemeral Resources and Write-only Arguments; this part is about how they apply to Google Cloud resources.

Where secrets leak

The usual ways a Terraform project leaks a secret on Google Cloud, in order of how often they happen, are:

Anti-pattern Better

A password or API key written as a literal in a .tf file, committed to Git

A variable with no default, supplied through a TF_VAR_ environment variable, a secret store, or an ephemeral read. See Variables, Outputs and Locals.

A terraform.tfvars file with secret values, committed or copied between machines

.tfvars files for non-secret settings only; ignore files that hold anything else.

secret_data on google_secret_manager_secret_version, a password on google_sql_user, a google_service_account_key, a tls_private_key, a google_sql_ssl_cert

These write the value into state in plain text. Use the write-only arguments (secret_data_wo, password_wo), generate or read values outside Terraform, or avoid keys altogether.

State in a bucket that many people can read, or a state file archived by CI as an artefact

A restricted, encrypted, versioned bucket with locking; never archive state.

Marking a variable sensitive and believing it is out of state

sensitive only hides values in CLI output. The value is still stored in state and in saved plans unless the argument is write-only.

Source: Terraform Docs — Manage sensitive data and Google Cloud — Best practices for security

Secret Manager

A secret has two parts in Secret Manager and in Terraform. The secret (google_secret_manager_secret) is a named container with replication, labels, rotation and expiry settings. A version (google_secret_manager_secret_version) holds the payload. Terraform can manage both, but the payload is the part that must stay out of state. The service itself is covered in Secret Manager and KMS.

The arguments of the secret that matter most:

Argument Effect

secret_id and replication

The ID, and either auto {} (Google chooses the replication) or user_managed with explicit replicas, optionally with a customer-managed key per replica.

ttl or expire_time

Make the secret expire (a duration in seconds such as 2592000s, or an RFC 3339 timestamp). Only one can be set. They are for temporary secrets: a database password that expires silently takes the application down.

version_destroy_ttl

A delay between a destroy request on a version and its real destruction. During the delay the version is disabled, which gives a window to notice a mistake.

rotation and topics

Secret Manager publishes a notification to the configured Pub/Sub topics at next_rotation_time and then every rotation_period. It does not rotate anything by itself; something must subscribe, create a new version and change the system the secret protects. topics must be set for rotation.

annotations, labels, tags

Metadata. Annotations and labels are non-authoritative, like other labels in this provider.

deletion_protection

Prevents Terraform from destroying the secret; defaults to false.

Source: Terraform Registry — google_secret_manager_secret

For the payload there are two options. secret_data is sensitive in plan output but is stored in state. secret_data_wo is write-only: it is sent to the API and never stored, so a rotation is expressed by changing secret_data_wo_version, which Terraform does store and compare. The two are mutually exclusive. Provider 8.0.0 changed the contract: secret_data_wo_version became a string (existing state converts on the first apply), and it is required whenever secret_data_wo is set, with the old implicit default of 0 removed. If your configuration still has an integer there, quote it before upgrading.

variable "reviews_api_key" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
  ephemeral = true
}

resource "google_secret_manager_secret" "reviews_api_key" {
  project   = var.project_id
  secret_id = "bookshelf-${var.environment}-reviews-api-key"

  replication {
    auto {}
  }

  version_destroy_ttl = "86400s"

  topics {
    name = google_pubsub_topic.secret_events.id
  }

  rotation {
    rotation_period    = "7776000s" # 90 days
    next_rotation_time = "2027-01-15T00:00:00Z"
  }
}

resource "google_pubsub_topic" "secret_events" {
  project = var.project_id
  name    = "bookshelf-${var.environment}-secret-events"
}

resource "google_secret_manager_secret_version" "reviews_api_key" {
  secret                 = google_secret_manager_secret.reviews_api_key.id
  secret_data_wo         = var.reviews_api_key
  secret_data_wo_version = "1"
  deletion_policy        = "DISABLE"
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_secret_manager_secret_version

For rotation notifications to be delivered, the Secret Manager service agent needs roles/pubsub.publisher on the topic, as the provider documents; that agent can be created with google_project_service_identity (a beta resource, as described below) and granted with google_pubsub_topic_iam_member.

Run it with TF_VAR_reviews_api_key in the environment (it is never printed because the variable is both sensitive and ephemeral), and increment secret_data_wo_version (a string) when you want a new version. deletion_policy set to DISABLE makes terraform destroy disable the version instead of destroying it, and ABANDON leaves it alone; the default destroys.

Two lifecycle points deserve care when secret_data (not the write-only argument) is used. Changing the data replaces the version resource, so a plain replacement destroys the old version before the new one exists unless you ask for the other order with lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }; with that setting consumers that read latest never see a moment with no enabled version. And a secret that has a ttl or expire_time will disappear on schedule even though Terraform still lists it, so treat the expiry as part of the contract, not as a clean-up.

Reading secrets back into Terraform has the same two options. The google_secret_manager_secret_version data source puts the payload into state; the ephemeral resource with the same name does not (see the Cloud SQL user earlier). The only legitimate reason to use the data source is a value that is not secret.

Cloud KMS and customer-managed encryption keys

Google encrypts data at rest by default. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) in Cloud KMS give you control of the key’s rotation, disablement and audit trail, and satisfy policies that require it. They are configured per resource: Cloud Storage buckets (encryption.default_kms_key_name), Cloud SQL (encryption_key_name), Pub/Sub topics (kms_key_name), BigQuery datasets (default_encryption_configuration), Secret Manager (customer_managed_encryption with kms_key_name, inside replication) and the state backend (kms_encryption_key).

Three properties of Cloud KMS shape the Terraform code. A key ring and a key cannot be deleted from a project; destroying the Terraform resource only removes it from state, and for a key it also deletes the key versions, after which anything encrypted with it is unrecoverable (versions pass through a scheduled-destruction period, 30 days by default, configurable with destroy_scheduled_duration when the key is created). The rotation_period must be longer than a day. And each Google service that uses your key does so through its own service agent, which must be granted roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the key, before the dependent resource is created.

resource "google_kms_key_ring" "bookshelf" {
  project  = var.project_id
  name     = "bookshelf-${var.environment}"
  location = var.region
}

resource "google_kms_crypto_key" "data" {
  name            = "data"
  key_ring        = google_kms_key_ring.bookshelf.id
  purpose         = "ENCRYPT_DECRYPT"
  rotation_period = "7776000s"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}

data "google_storage_project_service_account" "gcs" {
  project = var.project_id
}

resource "google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member" "gcs" {
  crypto_key_id = google_kms_crypto_key.data.id
  role          = "roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter"
  member        = "serviceAccount:${data.google_storage_project_service_account.gcs.email_address}"
}

resource "google_storage_bucket" "exports" {
  project                     = var.project_id
  name                        = "bookshelf-exports-${var.environment}-${var.project_id}"
  location                    = var.region
  uniform_bucket_level_access = true
  public_access_prevention    = "enforced"

  encryption {
    default_kms_key_name = google_kms_crypto_key.data.id
  }

  depends_on = [google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.gcs]
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_kms_crypto_key, google_storage_bucket and google_kms_crypto_key_iam

The key and the bucket must be in compatible locations. For services whose service agent is not exposed by a data source, the google_project_service_identity resource creates it. At the time of writing that resource is documented as beta, so it needs provider = google-beta, and once created it cannot be updated or destroyed (those actions do nothing). This is the typical reason to keep a google-beta provider block in an otherwise GA configuration:

resource "google_project_service_identity" "cloudsql" {
  provider = google-beta

  project = var.project_id
  service = "sqladmin.googleapis.com"
}

resource "google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member" "cloudsql" {
  crypto_key_id = google_kms_crypto_key.data.id
  role          = "roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter"
  member        = google_project_service_identity.cloudsql.member
}

# Then on the instance: encryption_key_name = google_kms_crypto_key.data.id

Source: Terraform Registry — google_project_service_identity

Encryption in transit is configured separately and was shown earlier: ssl_mode = ENCRYPTED_ONLY on Cloud SQL, HTTPS-only Cloud Run endpoints, private Google access on subnets, and storage_custom_endpoint for the state backend.

IAM: authoritative or not

Google Cloud IAM resources in the provider come in three flavours for every kind of resource, and mixing them is the most common source of surprising plans:

Resource Behaviour

*_iam_policy

Authoritative for the whole policy of the target: replaces everything, including bindings added by other tools or by Google. Use it only on resources you fully own; on a project it can lock you out.

*_iam_binding

Authoritative for one role on the target: the members listed are the members, others are removed.

*_iam_member

Non-authoritative: adds one member to one role and leaves everything else alone. The default choice.

Source: Terraform Registry — google_project_iam

Together with the earlier advice, the practical rules are: grant roles with the member form; scope each grant as narrowly as possible (a role on a secret, a bucket, a service or a repository beats a role on the project); use predefined roles, and a custom role only when no predefined role fits; and never grant the basic Owner, Editor or Viewer roles to workloads. The provider’s member attribute on google_service_account produces the right serviceAccount: string.

A custom role and a conditional grant look like this. IAM conditions use Common Expression Language and apply to the binding they are attached to; the example grants a contractor temporary read access to logs.

resource "google_project_iam_custom_role" "bookshelf_operator" {
  project     = var.project_id
  role_id     = "bookshelfOperator"
  title       = "Bookshelf operator"
  description = "Restart Cloud Run revisions and read logs, nothing else"
  stage       = "GA"

  permissions = [
    "run.services.get",
    "run.services.list",
    "run.revisions.list",
    "logging.logEntries.list",
  ]
}

resource "google_project_iam_member" "contractor_logs" {
  project = var.project_id
  role    = "roles/logging.viewer"
  member  = "user:contractor@example.com"

  condition {
    title       = "expires-2027-01-01"
    description = "Temporary access for the audit"
    expression  = "request.time < timestamp(\"2027-01-01T00:00:00Z\")"
  }
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_project_iam_custom_role and google_project_iam

The role_id of a custom role is camel case and cannot contain a hyphen. Custom roles are for a project or an organization and need stage to say whether they are in alpha, beta or general availability. The permissions list must be checked against the permissions the services actually need; use the IAM Recommender and the audit logs rather than guesswork.

The external data source, which the book uses to compute IAM values with scripts, is an escape hatch with a clear protocol: a program reads a JSON object of strings from standard input and prints a JSON object of strings on standard output, and runs on every refresh. Its documentation warns that it hurts portability and that it is not recommended in Terraform Enterprise. Almost everything IAM needs is available through provider resources and data sources (for example google_iam_policy, google_project, google_service_account), so reach for external last.

Source: Terraform Registry — external data source

Securing the remote state

The state bucket is the most sensitive object of the whole configuration. Most of the work is in the bootstrap section; the checklist below connects the controls to Google’s guidance.

  • Access: only the deployer service accounts and a small administrator group hold roles/storage.objectAdmin or higher on the bucket. Developers get plan-only identities (read-only roles on resources, and the permission to read the state) if the pipeline cannot run plans for them.

  • Encryption: the default Google-managed encryption always applies; add a customer-managed key through kms_encryption_key for stricter control. Google’s security page also mentions customer-supplied keys through GOOGLE_ENCRYPTION_KEY, with the migration limitations described earlier. OpenTofu can additionally encrypt state client side.

  • Locking: provided by the backend; do not disable it with -lock=false in automation.

  • Versioning and soft delete: on, with a lifecycle cap, so recovery is possible without unbounded cost.

  • Audit: Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage record reads of state objects; see the audit section below.

  • Separation: one bucket (or at least one prefix and IAM boundary) per trust boundary, as Google’s separation-of-duties guidance says. A network team’s state should not be readable by the application team that merely consumes its outputs.

  • Not in the repository: ignore .terraform/, *.tfstate* and saved plans, which hold the same secrets.

Source: Google Cloud — Best practices for security

Audit logs, sinks and alerts

Google Cloud writes Admin Activity audit logs for administrative operations without configuration. Data Access audit logs, which record reads of data and of configuration, are disabled by default for all services except some BigQuery ones, are billed as log volume, and must be turned on per service, for example for Cloud Storage and Secret Manager. In Terraform that is google_project_iam_audit_config; a sink (google_logging_project_sink) routes matching log entries to a destination, and an alert policy reacts to metrics.

resource "google_project_iam_audit_config" "secrets_and_storage" {
  for_each = toset(["secretmanager.googleapis.com", "storage.googleapis.com"])

  project = var.project_id
  service = each.key

  audit_log_config {
    log_type = "DATA_READ"
  }

  audit_log_config {
    log_type = "DATA_WRITE"
  }
}

resource "google_storage_bucket" "audit_logs" {
  project                     = var.project_id
  name                        = "bookshelf-audit-${var.environment}-${var.project_id}"
  location                    = var.region
  uniform_bucket_level_access = true
  public_access_prevention    = "enforced"

  lifecycle_rule {
    condition {
      age = 365
    }
    action {
      type = "Delete"
    }
  }
}

resource "google_logging_project_sink" "audit" {
  project                = var.project_id
  name                   = "bookshelf-audit"
  destination            = "storage.googleapis.com/${google_storage_bucket.audit_logs.name}"
  filter                 = "logName:\"cloudaudit.googleapis.com\""
  unique_writer_identity = true
}

# A unique writer identity needs access to the destination.
resource "google_storage_bucket_iam_member" "audit_writer" {
  bucket = google_storage_bucket.audit_logs.name
  role   = "roles/storage.objectCreator"
  member = google_logging_project_sink.audit.writer_identity
}

resource "google_monitoring_notification_channel" "oncall" {
  project      = var.project_id
  display_name = "Bookshelf on-call"
  type         = "email"

  labels = {
    email_address = "oncall@example.com"
  }
}

resource "google_monitoring_alert_policy" "database_cpu" {
  project      = var.project_id
  display_name = "Bookshelf database CPU high"
  combiner     = "OR"

  conditions {
    display_name = "Cloud SQL CPU above 80 percent for 10 minutes"

    condition_threshold {
      filter          = "metric.type=\"cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/cpu/utilization\" AND resource.type=\"cloudsql_database\""
      comparison      = "COMPARISON_GT"
      threshold_value = 0.8
      duration        = "600s"

      aggregations {
        alignment_period   = "60s"
        per_series_aligner = "ALIGN_MEAN"
      }
    }
  }

  notification_channels = [google_monitoring_notification_channel.oncall.id]
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_logging_project_sink, google_project_iam (audit config) and google_monitoring_alert_policy

Three notes. First, project_iam_audit_config is authoritative for a given service: it replaces the existing audit configuration of that service, so declare it in one place only. Second, the sink’s writer_identity is only known after creation, which is why the bucket grant is a separate resource; the sink can start before the grant exists and drop entries until it does, so keep the dependency. Third, the metric type and resource type in the filter are those of Cloud SQL; check them against the Metrics Explorer for the service you alert on. The monitoring section of the Google Cloud pages, Monitoring and observability, covers metrics, log-based metrics and uptime checks in depth. Security Health Analytics, mentioned in Google’s best practices as a post-apply audit, and gcloud beta terraform vet as a pre-apply check, are the Google-native counterparts of the scanners in Code Quality and Security Scanning.

Resilience and recovery

A Terraform configuration is a recovery plan for infrastructure, not for data. Plan for four kinds of loss:

Loss Mechanism

The database

Automated backups with a retention count, point-in-time recovery, regional high availability, and a read replica in another region for disaster recovery (all shown above). Restoring is an operation on the instance, not a Terraform action.

A VM’s disk

A snapshot schedule: a google_compute_resource_policy with a snapshot_schedule_policy (a daily schedule, a retention in days, snapshot labels and storage location), attached to each disk with google_compute_disk_resource_policy_attachment. on_source_disk_delete defaults to KEEP_AUTO_SNAPSHOTS.

Objects

Versioning and soft delete on the bucket, a lifecycle rule that caps the versions, and a backup bucket in a different location that a transfer job or the application fills. Lifecycle rules can also move old objects to colder storage classes with SetStorageClass.

The configuration and the state

Git for the former, a versioned bucket for the latter; the whole project can be rebuilt by applying the layers in order against an empty project. Test that claim in a throwaway project at least once.

Source: Terraform Registry — google_compute_resource_policy and google_storage_bucket

DNS plays a part in failover: users reach the Bookshelf through a name, so keep the TTL of the records that point at it low enough that a switch to another region takes effect quickly, and manage the zone and record sets in their own layer (google_dns_managed_zone, google_dns_record_set) so that rebuilding an application layer never touches them. Cloud DNS is described in Cloud DNS and certificates.

Clean up

Everything above creates billable resources: Cloud SQL with high availability and a replica, Cloud Run, Pub/Sub, BigQuery, Cloud KMS keys, VMs and buckets. Destroy a practice environment as soon as you finish. Because the examples deliberately resist deletion, destroying them is a short procedure, not a single command.

  1. Lower the protections first, and apply that change. Protection arguments are checked against state, so changing them and destroying in one step does not work. The arguments are deletion_protection on google_cloud_run_v2_service, google_sql_database_instance, google_bigquery_table and google_container_cluster; settings.deletion_protection_enabled on Cloud SQL; force_destroy on buckets that still hold objects; and deletion_policy where it is PREVENT. The simplest way is a variable that every protected resource reads.

  2. Destroy the layers in reverse order: observability, apps, data, network, bootstrap.

  3. Deal with the resources that cannot be deleted. Cloud KMS key rings and keys stay in the project; destroying the Terraform resource schedules the key versions for destruction (30 days by default) and makes anything encrypted with the key unrecoverable. If the key must outlive the configuration, forget it with a removed block instead.

  4. Handle the private services connection. The VPC peering behind google_service_networking_connection is not a separate resource and can block deletion of the network. Set deletion_policy to REMOVE_PEERING (or ABANDON, which leaves the peering in place) and apply before destroying.

  5. Destroy the state bucket last, after migrating the bootstrap configuration’s state back to local.

variable "protect_resources" {
  type    = bool
  default = true
}

# On each protected resource:
#   deletion_protection = var.protect_resources
#   (Cloud SQL also: settings { deletion_protection_enabled = var.protect_resources })
#   (buckets: force_destroy = !var.protect_resources)

resource "google_service_networking_connection" "private_services" {
  network                 = google_compute_network.bookshelf.id
  service                 = "servicenetworking.googleapis.com"
  reserved_peering_ranges = [google_compute_global_address.private_services.name]
  deletion_policy         = var.protect_resources ? "DELETE" : "REMOVE_PEERING"
}

# Keep the encryption key, drop it from state
removed {
  from = google_kms_crypto_key.data

  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}

Source: Terraform Registry — google_service_networking_connection, google_kms_crypto_key and Terraform Docs — removed block

# 1. Apply the unprotected settings
terraform apply -var="protect_resources=false"

# 2. Destroy each layer, last created first
for layer in observability apps data network; do
  (cd "environments/dev/${layer}" && terraform destroy -var="protect_resources=false")
done

# 3. Bootstrap: move its state back to local, then destroy the state bucket
cd bootstrap
# remove the backend block from the configuration, then:
terraform init -migrate-state
terraform destroy -var="protect_resources=false"

# 4. Infrastructure Manager deployments created for the exercise
gcloud infra-manager deployments delete \
  "projects/my-project-id/locations/us-central1/deployments/bookshelf-covers"
gcloud infra-manager previews delete \
  "projects/my-project-id/locations/us-central1/previews/bookshelf-covers-preview"

# 5. Check nothing billable is left
gcloud run services list --project=my-project-id
gcloud sql instances list --project=my-project-id
gcloud storage buckets list --project=my-project-id
gcloud kms keyrings list --location=us-central1 --project=my-project-id

Source: Terraform Docs — terraform destroy and Infrastructure Manager — Delete deployments

For a throwaway project, shutting the whole project down removes everything at once, with a recovery window before final deletion; a google_project managed by Terraform has deletion_policy defaulting to PREVENT since 6.0.0, so set it to DELETE first, or use ABANDON to drop it from state. Delete Artifact Registry repositories, Cloud Logging buckets and the audit bucket if the destroy skipped them, and remember that secrets, keys and BigQuery data may have retention periods.

What changed recently

When Change

Provider 5.16.0, 6.0.0

The goog-terraform-provisioned attribution label: opt-in in 5.16.0, added to new resources by default from 6.0.0.

Terraform 1.10, 1.11

Ephemeral resources, variables and outputs (1.10) and write-only arguments (1.11). Provider 6.23.0 added password_wo to google_sql_user, and the Google provider gained ephemeral resources for tokens, keys and Secret Manager versions.

August 2024

Cloud Functions 2nd generation became Cloud Run functions; the Terraform resource is still google_cloudfunctions2_function.

Provider 6.0.0 (2024-08-26)

Deletion protection on Cloud Run v2 services and jobs, project deletion_policy defaulting to PREVENT, ssl_mode instead of require_ssl.

Provider 6.28.0 (2025-04-01)

external_credentials in the provider block.

2025-03-18

Container Registry shut down; use Artifact Registry.

Provider 7.0.0 (2025-08-26)

disable_on_destroy without default, event_type required on 2nd generation functions, password_wo and password_wo_version as a pair.

2026-04-01

Deployment Manager support discontinued; Infrastructure Manager is the replacement.

Provider 8.0.0 (2026-08-26)

Removed BeyondCorp, IAP brand and client, ML Engine and notebooks resources; secret_data_wo_version required and a string; EXTERNAL_MANAGED as the default load balancing scheme.

Provider 8.8.0 (2026-10-21)

Latest at the time of writing; adds google_cloud_run_v2_instance and its IAM resources among others.

Source: terraform-provider-google changelog and Artifact Registry — Transition from Container Registry

Terraform and OpenTofu on Google Cloud

The Google providers are the same code for both tools, installed from the Terraform registry or the OpenTofu registry, and authentication, impersonation and federation behave identically. The differences are around them:

  • The OpenTofu gcs backend documents one more argument, universe_domain, and OpenTofu adds client-side state and plan encryption, which can be combined with the bucket’s own encryption.

  • Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform; its documentation lists only Terraform versions, so OpenTofu cannot be selected there.

  • Module version constraints compare version numbers of the tool. The Fabric modules require Terraform >= 1.12.2; the numbers of OpenTofu and Terraform are not comparable, so test modules with the tool you use instead of trusting the constraint.

Where the book is outdated or wrong

  • hashicorp/google pinned exactly to 5.38.0 (Wang). Use the current major with a ~> constraint and the lock file.

  • Retired resources and images (Wang): google_cloudfunctions_function (1st generation), google_cloud_run_service, gcr.io images, debian-10, and MySQL 5.7. Use google_cloudfunctions2_function, google_cloud_run_v2_service, Artifact Registry, debian-13 and a current PostgreSQL or MySQL major.

  • A service account with the editor role plus a downloaded JSON key (Wang). Use least-privilege roles with impersonation and Workload Identity Federation.

  • secret_data stored in state (Wang). Use write-only arguments and ephemeral reads.

  • GKE master authorized networks open to everyone (Wang). Restrict them to real administrator ranges.

  • A gcs backend with key and region (Wang). The backend takes bucket and prefix.

  • state pull and state push to adopt a remote backend (Wang). Use terraform init -migrate-state.

  • tf.tfvars loaded automatically (Wang). Only terraform.tfvars, terraform.tfvars.json and .auto.tfvars files are.

Pitfalls

  • Pinning nothing, or everything: use ~> constraints, commit the lock file, and read the upgrade guide before a major.

  • Destroying a google_project_service on a provider older than 7.0.0 with the default disable_on_destroy.

  • Leaving edition unset on PostgreSQL 16 or later with a custom tier.

  • Applying a Cloud Run change that CI also deploys, so each tool reverts the other’s image.

  • Granting roles/run.invoker to allUsers by habit.

  • Expecting a *_iam_policy resource to add to existing policy; it replaces it.

  • Using GOOGLE_CREDENTIALS for the provider and forgetting that the backend reads it too.

  • Deploying modules with a newer Terraform floor to Infrastructure Manager.

  • Forgetting that a destroyed KMS key makes data unrecoverable.

  • Running the first apply of an ephemeral secret read before the secret has a version.
